verdicts.note: Example used V/R before Ohm's law is taught; reworded to the qualitative rule (more resistance, less current).
Removed the claim that a Li-ion cell holds more energy than an alkaline AA of the same size; false for AA-size (14500) Li-ion cells. Replaced with the safe rechargeable contrast.
Mentioned a continuity test before that term is taught two cards later; replaced with a layout check.
Electrons and protons were used without saying what they are; now particles in atoms. 'So they look neutral' now 'are neutral overall'.

Wrong: Tip said the charge in everyday gadgets is a small fraction of a coulomb, so milli- and microcoulombs are common; a 1000 mAh cell holds 3600 C, as electricity-capacity-mah says. Now: static charge is a tiny fraction of a coulomb, but 1 A moves 1 C every second.
Added that Q/t is the average current when the flow is not steady.
Repeated numeracy-convert-milliamps and numeracy-charge-from-current-time (same 20 mA sensor, same 0.1 C answer); now 20 mA for one minute = 1.2 C, with the electron count tying in the coulomb card.

'Where does it break down' had several right answers; the title now asks how a break in a wire differs from a cut pipe. 'Water pressure' now 'pressure difference', since voltage is between two points. Defined 'circuit', first used on the next card.
Defined 'terminal' at its first use. 'Moving ground' could be read as rewiring; now 'which point you call ground'.
Answer line 'gives up energy in the lamp, not itself' was garbled; rewritten. 'Charge can't vanish or pile up' now scoped to a steady circuit (the balloon on card 1 shows charge can pile up).

Wrong: 'Every formula and diagram in electronics uses conventional current' (electron-flow textbooks exist); now 'almost every'. '+ to −' holds only outside the battery; added that it runs from − to + inside. 'maths' to 'math'.
Conductor and insulator are materials, but the card gave them a resistance; now a copper wire has very low resistance.
'Two-legged' excluded leg-less surface-mount resistors; now 'two-terminal'. Color bands scoped to resistors with wire legs. American spelling.

Wrong reasoning: the Why derived Ohm's law from the definition R = V/I, which makes it a tautology; the law is that R stays constant (at a steady temperature), which electricity-led-not-ohmic relies on. The answer line now states that condition.

Answer line defined a short only as a path across the supply and said every short makes the current huge, while its own Watch out shorts a single part, which need not raise the current much. Now general, with the across-the-supply case. Defined 'supply' (first use); added the fire risk with a big battery.

Wrong typical value: a red LED does not 'start conducting at about 2 V'; near 2 V it already passes its ~20 mA working current (Kingbright red: 1.85 V typ at 20 mA) and half a volt lower it passes almost nothing. Added that the threshold applies when connected the right way round.
No accepted answer with the unit; added '20 mA', as the numeracy module does.
Added accepted answers '300 ohm', '300 ohms' and '300 Ω'.
E = P·t holds for a steady power; condition added.

Unstated condition: 'doubling the current quadruples the heat' holds only in the same resistor; at a fixed voltage, doubling the current by halving R only doubles the power. Added 'in the same resistor'.

Rule of thumb stated as always true ('a bigger rating means a physically bigger resistor', now 'usually'), and the rating was given without its condition: it assumes the resistor can shed its heat, so a hot enclosure lowers it. Glossed 'headroom'.
Added accepted answer '495 mW'.
Added accepted answer '9000 J'.
Wrong: said a 1/2 W resistor 'could burn out' at 0.44 W, which is within its rating. Now only the 1/4 W part is overloaded; the 1/2 W one runs hot with almost no margin.

The title asks what nodes and branches are, but the answer line did not say; added. Node definition aligned with circuits-node-and-loop: points joined by plain wire count as one node, so a parallel circuit has two nodes however many junctions it has.

Mnemonic 'Series shares current' used 'share' in the opposite sense from the explanation ('each part's share is its voltage drop'); now 'Series: same current. Parallel: same voltage.' Drops add up to the supply only when the chain is the only loop; condition added.
Moved ahead of the parallel formula (README order: example before formula; difficulty 1 before 2). It now defines equivalent resistance, which its title uses.
The definition of equivalent resistance moved to the series example that now comes first.
'Load' was used without definition (first use); defined.
Added accepted answer '6 V'.
Added accepted answers '2 kohm', '2k' and '2 kΩ'.
Key idea used 'capacity' a card before it is defined; reworded. A cell turns stored chemical energy into electrical energy rather than just storing it.
'The label is an ideal' mischaracterized the rating, which is measured under the maker's test conditions; added that capacity also depends on the lowest voltage the device can still run on.
Used 'nominal voltage' a card before it is defined; defined it inline and noted the result is an estimate.

Fresh alkaline AA value tightened to 1.5 to 1.6 V (new cells measure about 1.57 to 1.65 V open circuit) and the end point to 'about 1 V or below' (Energizer rates capacity to 0.8 V). Glossed 'alkaline'; 'labelled' to 'labeled'.

Wrong: defined a coin cell as non-rechargeable, but rechargeable coin cells exist (LIR2032, 3.6 V); now only the CR2032 is. A numbers card must state its conditions: added the rating basis (about 0.2 mA, down to 2.0 V, room temperature; Panasonic 225 mAh, Energizer 235 mAh). Removed the undefined 'datasheet'. Added datasheet URLs; asOf updated.

Values scoped to cobalt- and nickel-based cells, and LiFePO4 now described as also lithium-ion (3.2 V nominal, 3.65 V full, per Battery University BU-216, added as a ref). Glossed 'ions' and 'electrodes'.
'Ideal voltage source' was undefined; glossed. Added concrete values: about 0.2 ohm for a fresh alkaline AA (Energizer E91: 150 to 300 mohm), roughly 10 to 20 ohm for a fresh CR2032.
Tip 'between 70% and 80% is a common choice' did not say of what (a 70% margin would mean counting on 30%); now the share of rated capacity you count on. Added accepted answers '16 h' and '16 hours'.
Warned that the C of C-rate is not the coulomb, which this module writes as C. '1C drains the cell in one hour' now 'ideally'.
Added that lines crossing without a dot are not joined, the classic trap. The long-and-short pair is strictly a cell; a battery may show several pairs.
'Soldering' was used without definition; glossed.

Used 'continuity' five cards before the continuity test is taught (the defect round 1 fixed on the breadboard card); now explained on the spot. Not every multimeter is handheld; glossed 'probes'; replaced the unverifiable 'most meter mistakes come from a wrong setting'.
Added that an open switch is off, the reverse of a water tap; beginners often read 'opening the switch' the other way.

'Left and right halves' assumed one board orientation while electricity-rails-not-powered said 'top and bottom' rails; both are now orientation-free. Glossed 'chip', 'pins' and 'jumper wire' at first use. American spelling.
Defined a voltmeter and an ammeter as 'a multimeter measuring...'; they are any meter for voltage or current, a multimeter on that setting being one.

Safety: said the fuse always blows and protects the meter, but many cheap (DT830-style) meters have an unfused 10 A socket, where a short can damage the meter or overheat the battery; added, with the trap of leaving the red probe in a current socket. Defined 'fuse'; the example now names the milliamp socket.
'Top and bottom rail pairs' now 'the rail pairs along the two long edges', consistent with the holes card. Replaced the undefined 'live'. American spelling.
